title: The press in the browser
summary: A case study of ProPre Engine, the browser tool that takes a coloring book from first prompt to print-ready cover, and the project that brought me back to web development.

post.title: The press in the browser
post.body:
This is the project that brought me back to web development after a long break. I'd started making adult coloring books, and every one of them meant the same pile of jobs: prompts for 40 illustrations, a listing with titles and keywords, an interior PDF with the right bleed, a wraparound cover whose spine depends on the page count, and a separate cover for the ebook. I wanted one place that did all of it.

Here's the idea underneath it. A coloring book is beauty broken down to its most basic form, then built back up. Every page starts as a beautiful picture: that picture is the core of each prompt, crafted almost. Then it's taken apart, the way a prism splits light, until only the black and white lines are left. And the person with the markers fills it back in, in their own colours.

So I wrote down what it should be. The first notes are dated May 20. Two days later there were eight single-page prototypes. By May 24 there was a working tool of about 100 KB. Within the week I'd split it into modules with a small build script, because one file had become too big to change safely, and written a full set of documents for it: a product spec, a requirements spec, technical docs and a user manual.

I called it ProPre, for pre-press. It has five tabs. The Prompt Generator takes an object, a lens like Through the Seasons or Underwater, and an edition for adults or kids, and writes the brief for a prompt catalog. Long books run in two halves, pages 1 to 20 and 21 to 40. MegaData writes the listing in one go: titles, subtitles, back copy, seven keywords, an HTML description and the series copy. Interior turns a zip of line art into the print PDF, in double-sided, right-handed or left-handed editions. Cover builds the wraparound PDF and works out the spine from the page count. Kindle Cover makes the ebook cover with a live preview.

Every one of those steps has a rule I learned the hard way. Text stays inside the safe zone. Art is scaled a little past the page so it really fills the bleed. Interiors are black and white only. Covers are cropped, never stretched. Prompts stay clear of anything trademarked.

Then the books needed a home, so I built the Coloring Book Catalog. It reads a spreadsheet, so adding a book is adding a row. 101 titles so far, 8 in print and 93 on the way. Each card shows the line art, and a tap fills it with colour.

This week I gave it a proper repository. The live page had drifted ahead of its own source files, so the sources were rebuilt from it until a build matched the live page byte for byte. Its AI calls now go through the Studio's login instead of a token in the page.

What I learned: build the tool before the hundredth book, not after. Every rule I wrote into ProPre is a mistake I only had to make once, and every one of them protects the same thing: the beautiful picture at the start, so there's something worth building back up at the end.

episode.title: The press in the browser
episode.script:
This is where it all started.

Christian had been away from web development for a long while. What brought him back was coloring books. Adult coloring books, the detailed, beautiful kind.

Every book is a mountain of small jobs. Forty illustrations, each one needing its own prompt. A listing with titles and keywords. The inside pages, built just so for printing. A cover that wraps around the whole book, with a spine that changes width with the page count. And a second cover for the ebook. Most people would just push through it. He didn't.

He describes a coloring book in a way I haven't forgotten. It's beauty, broken down to its bones. Every page starts as a beautiful picture, carefully crafted into the prompt. Then it's taken apart, like light through a prism, until nothing is left but black and white lines. And then you come along with your markers, and you build the beauty back up yourself.

***

On the twentieth of May, he wrote down what he wanted. Two days later there were eight little prototypes. By the twenty-fourth, a working tool. And within the week, a full set of proper documents, specs and a user manual and all.

That same week, he split the whole thing into tidy modules, because one big file had grown too big to change safely. It's the kind of decision nobody notices, and it saves everything later.

***

He called it ProPre, short for pre-press. Five tabs. One writes the prompts for the pictures. One writes the whole listing in one go, titles, keywords, everything. One builds the inside of the book. One builds the cover and works out the spine from the page count, so the math is never wrong. And one makes the ebook cover, with a live preview as you go.

Every step has a rule built in that he learned the hard way. Keep the words inside the safe edge. Make the art fill all the way to the trim. Never stretch a cover. Every rule in there is a mistake he only had to make once.

***

Then the books needed a home, so he built a library. A hundred and one titles. Eight in print, ninety-three on the way. Every card shows the line art, and when you tap it, it fills with color.

***

And this week, he gave the whole thing a proper home of its own, and locked the clever parts behind the Studio's door, where they belong.

Looking back, the lesson is plain. Build the tool before the hundredth book, not after.

consent: No people appear. The covers and pages are Christian's own books.

narratorLook.prompt: Same image, same camera, same face, same eyes, same jaw, same neck and the same flat chroma green background (#00B140). Change only the hair and accessories: her hair pulled up into a massive, crown-like pineapple updo of sculpted brass coils bursting out of the top of a snug open-crown cap in dark rose-gold, the coils piled high and full, with a few chunky ringlets falling at her temples. Her flower-bud antenna rises from the middle of the coils exactly where it is now. Polished brass and rose-gold; the tallest coils still stay inside the crop box. Bold, chunky shapes; nothing crosses her face below the brows; everything stays inside the crop box.
